WTO hikes global trade growth forecast, names Pakistan among nations gaining from disruptions amid ME conflict
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: The World Trade Organisation on Thursday sharply raised its global trade growth forecast for 2026 — with merchandise trade riding the AI boom — and concluded that some nations, including Pakistan, were actually benefiting from trade disruptions amid the ongoing Middle East conflict in some ways.

In its Global Trade Outlook Update 2026, the Geneva-based global trade watchdog said its economists had upgraded their forecasts for global merchandise trade volume growth to 3.9 per cent for 2026 and 4.1pc for 2027 — up from previous estimates of 1.9pc and 2.6pc, respectively, projected at the start of the US-Iran conflict in March.

The report said that despite the conflict, the global economy had remained resilient, reflecting a stronger-than-expected surge in AI-related capital investment and increased supplies of fuels and fertilisers from countries outside the Middle East.

While several countries faced fuel transport disruptions because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the redistribution of traffic was creating opportunities for various other economies, it said.

“For example, Pakistan’s exports of sea freight transport services rose by 73pc year-on-year in the first half of 2026, as its transport operators benefited from increased traffic,” the WTO said.

Vessel calls at major container terminals in Karachi were still 14pc higher year-on-year in July, it added.

Exports by the United States to the European Union continued to expand while exports to Asia and the Pacific decreased by 2pc in the second quarter.

At the same time, computer services exports by several smaller and emerging players expanded rapidly. In the second quarter, computer services exports from Malaysia rose by 34pc, those from Pakistan by 23pc and by 13pc in Brazil.

The WTO also noted that the rerouting of vessels and containers towards alternative ports and trans-shipment hubs had put pressure on capacity in South Asia, translating into higher charges. In July, the Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) introduced a congestion surcharge of $500 per container on shipments from Northern Europe to India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

“Longer waiting and transit times are increasing costs for carriers and traders, some of which may ultimately be passed on to consumers,” it said.

Stronger-than-expected growth reflects opposing forces

The report revised the forecast for commercial services trade volume growth in 2026 down to 3.3pc from the previous 4.8pc, as the conflict in the Middle East has depressed travel and tourism in the region and raised fuel input costs worldwide.

In 2027, growth rates in volume terms for merchandise and commercial services trade were expected to rise to 4.1pc and 6.4pc, respectively, but this outcome depended on a timely resolution of the Middle East conflict, according to the WTO.

Based on these projections, the volume of global goods and services trade was expected to grow by approximately 3.7pc in 2026 and 4.7pc in 2027, the organisation forecast.

The stronger-than-expected growth in merchandise trade reflects two opposing forces, according to the watchdog. On the one hand, the push from AI-related investment has increased demand for AI-enabling goods, which accounted for 47pc of global merchandise trade growth in value terms in the first half of 2026. On the other hand, reduced shipments of oil, natural gas and fertilisers have weighed on merchandise trade; for the ongoing year to date, the former has outweighed the latter, the WTO said.

It noted that while high commodity prices may persist as a result of bottlenecks constraining the flows of fuels and fertilisers, continued AI investment and the broader digitisation of the global economy were expected to keep merchandise trade growth above the rate of global GDP growth in 2027.

“AI investment and the Middle East conflict are also affecting the services trade outlook, but to different degrees. AI is lifting trade in computer and financial services. However, the impact of the conflict in the Middle East is prevailing in traditional services such as transport, tourism and construction,” it said.

Conversely, services trade growth is expected to remain below trend this year before rebounding in 2027. Asia and North America are expected to see their contributions decline, while those of Europe are expected to remain broadly stable, putting the region on track to account for over half of the growth in export services this year.

Meanwhile, the rest of the world was expected to make a negative contribution, dragged down by a large contraction in the Middle East, the report added. All services sub-sectors are expected to see growth below the March baseline forecast.

However, it noted that the trade forecast remains subject to several significant risks.

“The current wedge between crude oil and refined oil prices is weighing on trade growth by eroding households’ purchasing power. A slowdown or reversal of AI investment spending could also have a significant impact on trade given its high import content,” it said.

Turning to trade statistics in value terms, the WTO said the current US dollar value of world merchandise trade had risen considerably faster than volume in the first half of 2026, up 15pc year-on-year compared to 3.5pc growth in volume terms.

“This marks one of the largest gaps between the value and volume of trade growth in recent years, reflecting higher prices for fuels and electronic components for data centres,” it said.

It noted that trade continued to show “some alignment with geopolitical considerations”, although it pointed out that the gap between intra-bloc and inter-bloc trade had narrowed through 2025 and into 2026, suggesting that “the broader pattern of bloc-based fragmentation has not continued to intensify”.

US-China trade decoupling had, however, accelerated since 2025 and was now the main driver of the bloc divergence, it added.

UNHRC adopts first-ever resolution on AI; Bangladesh acts as penholder
item.description:
The United Nations Human Rights Council has adopted by consensus the first-ever resolution on artificial intelligence (AI), titled “Implications of Artificial Intelligence for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights”, with Bangladesh serving as the penholder and playing a leading role in advancing the initiative.
During the ongoing 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council, Bangladesh joined fellow Core Group members Algeria, Austria, Egypt, Greece, Guyana, Kuwait and Nepal in steering the initiative on AI and human rights.
Guided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh, the initiative was first presented before the Council in August 2026 by former Ambassador and Permanent Representative Nahida Sobhan on behalf of the Core Group.
Since then, the Core Group has pursued an open, inclusive and constructive process of engagement with Member States and relevant stakeholders.
The consensus adoption marks a significant step forward in strengthening the Council’s consideration of the evolving relationship between artificial intelligence and human rights, while keeping human dignity, development, inclusion and international cooperation at the centre.
It also reflects Bangladesh’s growing and constructive role in shaping international discussions at the intersection of emerging technologies, development and human rights, and its growing contribution to multilateral diplomacy.
Bangladesh underscored that continued constructive engagement and cooperation among Member States and stakeholders will remain essential as the initiative moves forward.

ECNEC approves 13 projects involving Tk 162 billion
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) today approved 13 projects involving total cost of Tk 162 billion, including a project to construct a 442-MW peak solar power plant at Rampal in Bagerhat.

Of the total project cost, Tk 106 billion will come from government funds, Tk 40.8 billion from project loans and Tk 15.2 billion from concerned agencies’ own funds.

The approval came at the 5th meeting of the ECNEC held at Bangladesh Secretariat with Prime Minister and ECNEC Chairman Tarique Rahman in the chair.

Of the approved 13 projects, 10 are new, two are revised and one involves extension of its implementation period.

State Minister for Planning Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki briefed reporters after the meeting at the NEC Conference Room in the city’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area.

Under the Tk 24.9 billion Rampal project, a 442-megawatt peak (MWp) solar power plant will be constructed at Rampal in Bagerhat, aimed at increasing renewable energy generation, diversifying the country’s primary fuel sources and reducing carbon emissions.

The Rampal 442 MWp Solar Power Plant Construction Project was proposed by the Power Division and will be implemented by the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB). The project will be financed by BPDB from its own with Tk 3.74 billion and from Power Sector Development Fund Tk 21.23 billion.

The Power Sector Development Fund loan would carry a 2 per cent interest rate, with a one-year grace period and a 16-year repayment period.
The Planning Commission recommended that the project be implemented from September 2026 to March 2029.

In its assessment, the Planning Commission said the project would increase renewable-energy-based electricity generation and contribute to the government’s target of raising renewable energy’s share of the total energy mix to 20 per cent by 2030.

Once the project is implemented, it would add 442 MW of electricity to the national grid. Currently the solar power generation in the country is 797 MW out of the total ongrid power generation capacity of 28,827 MW.

“The project will increase electricity generation based on renewable energy, which will help achieve the target of generating 20 per cent of electricity from renewable sources by 2030,” said the Planning Commission official.

The Planning Commission said the project would strengthen energy security by diversifying primary fuel sources and reduce carbon emissions.
The proposed plant will be built on 918.50 acres of land in Block-B of Rampal that BPDB had already acquired. The Planning Commission said the use of BPDB-owned land would eliminate the need for fresh land acquisition and reduce project costs.

Electricity generated by the solar plant will be transmitted through the existing transmission infrastructure associated with the nearby Rampal coal-fired power plant. The project summary said this would allow the plant to be implemented relatively quickly and at lower cost.

BPDB acquired a total of 1,834 acres in Rampal in 2012 for development of a coal-fired power plant. The land was divided into Block-A, covering 915.50 acres, and Block-B covering 918.50 acres.

Bangladesh-India Friendship Power Company (Pvt) Ltd’s Maitree Super Thermal Power Plant was built in Block-A, while Block-B remains under BPDB.

Land development and boundary-wall construction have already been completed in Block-B, according to the project document.

The proposed solar plant will use solar photovoltaic modules with a minimum capacity of 640 watts peak. The project will also install grid-tied inverters with a cumulative capacity of 360 MW, a pooling substation, a three-kilometre double-circuit 230-kV transmission line and three 230-kV bays, including one spare bay.

The largest component of the project cost, Tk 12.38 billion, or around 50 per cent, will go to solar photovoltaic modules and mounting structures.
Electrical equipment, including inverters, transformers and SCADA systems will cost Tk 7.32 billion.

The project summary said a feasibility study was conducted by the Infrastructure Investment Facilitation Company (IIFC) and found the project acceptable.

The project was included in the Annual Development Programme (ADP) for fiscal 2026-27 as an unapproved “green page” project.

The project is also aligned with the Five Year Strategic Framework for Reform and Development and the Sustainable Development Goal 7, which seeks to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all.

The day’s meeting also approved seven projects under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives.

The projects are - improving road infrastructure and drainage in 18 wards under five newly incorporated regions of Dhaka South City Corporation; upgrading important infrastructure in Rangpur City Corporation; rehabilitating damaged roads in Rangpur City Corporation, and constructing roads, drains and footpaths in zones one to eight of Gazipur City Corporation.

The other projects under the ministry include a project for women’s skills development and entrepreneurship creation through cooperatives; rural infrastructure development in Sirajganj, Bogura and Naogaon districts; and the Important Urban Infrastructure Development Project (2nd phase), which was approved in its second revised form.

The ECNEC also approved the third revised project for procuring 35 commercial and eight auxiliary vessels for Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Corporation (BIWTC) and constructing two new slipways under the Ministry of Shipping.

Under the Ministry of Railways, the committee approved the Railway Capacity Expansion Project for procuring 30 metre-gauge diesel-electric locomotives for Bangladesh Railway.

It also approved a project under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to renovate and modernise the purchased chancery building in Paris, France, to make it suitable for use.

Two projects under the Ministry of Road Transport and Bridges also received approval. One involves constructing the Second Karatoya Bridge at the 15th kilometre of the Bhajanpur (Nijbari)-Atorkhari-Mainaguri-Amtali-Mirgachh-Panchagarh (Z-5060) road.

The other is the second revised Thanchi-Rimakri-Madak-Likri Road Construction Project.

Meanwhile, the ECNEC meeting was informed about a project costing less than Tk 500 million that had already received approval from the Planning Minister.

The project involves re-excavating the Nandahar and Harabati rivers and Nunogola and Kharowa canals in Joypurhat district.

Ministers and State Ministers concerned attended the meeting while Planning Commission members and secretaries concerned were present.

French-Japanese duo wins Nobel for solving chemical asymmetry puzzle
item.description:
France’s Henri Kagan and Japan’s Kenso Soai on Wednesday won the Nobel chemistry prize for solving the mystery of why only one version of some molecules’ mirror-image forms appears in nature, a discovery decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.
The pair were honored “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis,” the jury said.
Like hands, all amino acids exist as two mirrored variants, but only one of them is found in the proteins in the body’s cells.
The other is rarely found in nature, a phenomenon known as “homochirality,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained.
Chemists have long wondered how that process occurs, and the two Nobel laureates’ discoveries have “enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality,” the jury said.
“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
“Their discoveries have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals,” the jury said.
Last year, the chemistry prize went to Japan’s Susumu Kitagawa, UK-born Richard Robson and American-Jordanian Omar Yaghi for developing a method of designing molecular structures.
The chemistry prize follows the physics prize, which on Tuesday honored Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for groundbreaking work using Antarctic ice to capture particles originating in the distant cosmos.
On Monday, the medicine prize was awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a prize for a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award -- the peace prize -- is due on Friday.
US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2-million prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline.
The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

item.title: Bangladesh to replace Pakistan in Asian Hockey Champions Trophy
item.description:
Bangladesh have accepted an invitation from the Asian Hockey Federation (AHF) to replace Pakistan in the Men’s Asian Hockey Champions Trophy 2026, scheduled to be held in India from October 27 to November 5.

The AHF on Friday announced the revised schedule for the tournament without Pakistan following the country’s decision to withdraw from the event after its request for a neutral venue was rejected.

The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) had formally approached the continental body, seeking either the relocation of the entire tournament or the staging of Pakistan’s matches at a neutral venue, citing the sensitive bilateral situation between Pakistan and India and concerns over the safety and dignity of players and officials.

Hockey India and the AHF turned down the proposal, insisting that the tournament would be held as scheduled at the designated venues in Jalandhar and Mohali. Following the decision, the PHF informed the AHF that Pakistan would not travel to India under the existing arrangements.

Bangladesh, named as one of the two reserve teams alongside Oman, were subsequently invited to fill the vacant slot and accepted the offer.

The revised six-team line-up comprises India, Japan, China, Malaysia, South Korea and Bangladesh. All league-stage matches will be played at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium in Jalandhar from October 27 to November 2, with the opening ceremony also scheduled at the venue.

The semi-finals will be held in Mohali on November 4, while the final is scheduled for November 5 at the Olympian Balbir Singh Senior International Hockey Stadium.

Defending champions India, who won the title in Chennai in 2023 and Hulunbuir, China, in 2024, will open their campaign against Bangladesh on October 27. The scheduled India-Pakistan encounter on November 1 in Jalandhar has been scrapped following Pakistan’s withdrawal.

First held in 2011, the Asian Champions Trophy has regularly featured the traditional rivalry between India and Pakistan. The two sides last met in the semi-finals of the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, where India secured a 4-3 victory before retaining the gold medal.

Pakistan had also withdrawn from the Junior World Cup held in India last year, citing similar concerns.

Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann had earlier indicated that Pakistan was expected to participate, referring to India’s policy of allowing neighbouring countries to compete in multi-nation sporting events.

Despite Pakistan’s withdrawal and Bangladesh’s inclusion, the organisers have confirmed that the tournament will proceed as planned. The event will mark the return of a major international hockey tournament to Punjab after nearly two decades.

The latest development highlights the continuing impact of political tensions on sporting ties between Pakistan and India, despite their longstanding association with hockey and efforts to promote the sport at the continental level.

item.title: Bangladesh-India joint working group meeting begins today: what will be discussed on trade
item.description:
The two-day meeting of the Bangladesh-India Joint Working Group began in New Delhi on Thursday morning. According to sources at the Ministry of Commerce, Bangladesh’s main priorities are removing obstacles at land ports, seeking a review of India’s duties on jute products, and restoring normal import and export operations.

A 10-member Bangladeshi delegation led by Ayesha Akter, additional secretary (FTA) at the Ministry of Commerce, travelled to New Delhi yesterday, Wednesday, to attend the meeting.

According to ministry sources, the meeting will discuss ways to reduce the trade deficit between the two countries, remove obstacles to the import and export of goods, and strengthen bilateral trade and economic ties.

India’s new duties on Bangladeshi jute products and Bangladesh’s restrictions on imports of Indian yarn will also receive particular attention.

Meeting held after 3 years

The previous meeting of the Bangladesh-India Joint Working Group was held in Dhaka on 26 and 27 September 2023. Before that, the 14th meeting took place in New Delhi on 2 and 3 March 2022.

Following the political change in Bangladesh in August 2024, tensions developed in relations between the two countries. This affected trade discussions as well. As a result, the regular meeting was not held as scheduled.

According to ministry sources, the meeting will discuss ways to reduce the trade deficit between the two countries, remove obstacles to the import and export of goods, and strengthen bilateral trade and economic ties.

Previous meetings discussed infrastructure development at land ports and integrated check posts, withdrawal of port-related restrictions, reopening border haats, transporting goods by rail and expanding regional connectivity.

Coordination and mutual recognition of product standards, a joint study on a Bangladesh-India Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, and keeping the Petrapole-Benapole check posts open 24 hours a day were also discussed.

Land trade declines amid restrictions

One of the major manifestations of tensions in the commercial relationship between the two countries has been the use of land ports. In April 2025, Bangladesh stopped allowing imports of Indian yarn through the Benapole, Bhomra, Sonamasjid, Banglabandha and Burimari land ports. Imports by sea were still allowed.

A few weeks later, India imposed restrictions on imports from Bangladesh by land of various products, including ready-made garments, processed food, plastics and PVC. In June that year, restrictions were also imposed on jute and certain textile products.

The restrictions affected export figures at Benapole land port. In fiscal year 2025–26, Bangladesh exported 189,358 tonnes of goods to India through the port, compared with 381,440 tonnes in the previous fiscal year.

Despite the decline in volume, export earnings remained almost unchanged. Export earnings through Benapole stood at $1.75 billion in fiscal year 2025–26, compared with $1.76 billion in the previous fiscal year.

New Indian duties on jute products

Ahead of the meeting, India’s imposition of new duties on Bangladeshi jute products has emerged as an issue. On 24 September, India’s Ministry of Finance set revised anti-dumping duties on jute yarn and twine, hessian fabric, jute sacks and sacking cloth imported from Bangladesh and Nepal.

For Bangladeshi jute yarn and twine, the highest duty has been set at $445 per tonne. India has said the new duty was not imposed following a fresh investigation. Rather, the rates were revised based on a mid-term review of the existing duties.

In addition, on 29 September, India’s Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) recommended imposing anti-dumping duties of up to $218 per tonne on PET film imported from five countries, including Bangladesh.

For Bangladesh’s Akij Biax Films, the proposed duty is $58 per tonne. However, the recommendation will not take effect until India’s Ministry of Finance issues a final notification.

Business community’s demands also on agenda

Before finalising the agenda for the New Delhi meeting, the Ministry of Commerce held a meeting with the country’s leading business organisations in May. Business leaders recommended withdrawing restrictions at land ports, removing non-tariff barriers and restoring the transshipment facility that had previously been cancelled.

Indian Deputy High Commissioner to Bangladesh Pavan Kumar Tulshidas Badhe met with leaders of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI) last month.

At the meeting, proposals were made to reduce tariff and non-tariff barriers and establish a joint business task force comprising business representatives from both countries.

Earlier, at a meeting in August between Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir and Indian High Commissioner to Dhaka Dinesh Trivedi, the reopening of border haats, increasing the capacity of land ports and withdrawing restrictions on imports of Indian yarn were discussed.

Bangladesh loses second place in garment exports to the US
item.description:
In the first half of this year (January-June), Bangladeshi apparel exports to the US market decreased by almost six per cent.

By the end of July, it increased to six and a half per cent.

However, in August, the rate of decline decreased, with apparel exports decreasing by 4.43 per cent.

During the same period, apparel exports from China and India to the United States declined by more than 29 and 26 per cent, respectively.

Even though the decline in apparel exports to the US market slightly decreased, Bangladesh lost its second position to China.

At the end of July, Bangladesh was the second largest apparel exporting country after Vietnam, followed by China.

However, by the end of August, China had taken over Bangladesh's second position.

Bangladesh is now in third place, with a difference of 240 million USD in apparel exports between Bangladesh and China.

This picture emerged from updated data published by the US Office of Textiles and Apparel (OTEXA). The data shows that in the first eight months of this year (January-August), US apparel imports decreased by 7.42 per cent.

During this time, US traders imported apparel worth 49 billion or 4,900 crore USD.

Analysing OTEXA’s data reveals that in the first eight months of this year, the volume of US apparel imports decreased by 8.98 per cent.

Consequently, the average price per square meter of apparel increased by 1.71 per cent, although the average price of apparel exported from Bangladesh decreased.

During the January-August period of this year, Bangladesh exported apparel worth 5.39 billion USD to the US market, which is 4.43 per cent less compared to the same period last year. The decline in Bangladesh's exports is almost 3 percentage points more than the overall decrease in US apparel imports.

Meanwhile, in terms of volume, Bangladesh exported 1.76 billion square meters of apparel in the first eight months of this year, which is almost 3 per cent less than the same period last year. During this time, the average price per square meter of apparel exported from Bangladesh was 3.07 USD, which is a decrease of 1.73 per cent compared to the same period last year.

Among the countries supplying apparel to the US market, China experienced the largest decline. In the first eight months of this year, China exported apparel worth 5.63 billion USD, which is a decrease of 29.39 per cent compared to the same period last year.

During the same period, India's exports decreased by 26.44 per cent, and Pakistan’s apparel exports decreased by 3.83 per cent. On the other hand, apparel exports from Indonesia and Cambodia increased by 2.58 per cent and 6.91 per cent, respectively.

Vietnam is the top apparel-exporting country to the US market. In the first eight months of this year, it exported apparel worth 10.98 billion USD, a decrease of 0. 76 per cent compared to the same period last year. The average price per square meter of apparel exported from Vietnam was 3. 54 USD, a 0.58 per cent decrease compared to last year.

Among the top 10 exporting countries, the price of Chinese apparel decreased by 9. 93 per cent. In the first eight months of this year, the average price per square meter of apparel exported from China was 1.47 USD, which is half the price of apparel from Bangladesh.

The price of apparel exported from Pakistan to the US from Bangladesh is also low, with the price per square meter equivalent apparel being 2.78 USD.

item.title: Australia provides Tk 1.55b to support Rohingyas, host communities in Bangladesh
item.description:
Australia has signed an AUD18 million (about Tk 1.55 billion) agreement with BRAC to support Rohingya refugees and host communities in Bangladesh.

Australian High Commissioner Susan Ryle and BRAC Executive Director Asif Saleh signed the agreement. The announcement was made in the presence of Disaster Management and Relief Minister Asadul Habib Dulu.

The funding will provide flexible, multi-year support for essential services for Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar and Bhasan Char, according to a press release issued by the Australian High Commission.

Under the agreement, BRAC will provide support in areas including healthcare, water and sanitation, education, disaster risk management, skills development and protection services in the refugee camps and surrounding host communities.

The programme will also support local organisations through BRAC’s localisation fund. The fund is intended to strengthen the capacity of national partners, support cost-effective delivery of services at scale and expand coverage in underserved camps, according to the release.

The new agreement is part of Australia’s AUD370 million (about Tk 31.6 billion) humanitarian package for 2026–2028. The package will support Rohingya refugees and host communities in Bangladesh as well as people affected by the crisis in Myanmar.

Since 2017, Australia has committed AUD1.26 billion (about Tk 107.7 billion) in humanitarian assistance in response to the regional crisis, the release said.

Australia remains committed to supporting the Bangladesh government in providing humanitarian assistance to displaced Rohingyas and their host communities, it said.

The Australian government said continued access to essential support for the Rohingya was critical until conditions are in place for their voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return to Myanmar.

item.title: CPA, DP World sign deal to boost Chittagong port capacity
item.description:
Chittagong Port Authority (CPA) and global port operator DP World on Thursday signed a 15-year concession agreement for the operation and modernisation of the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT), marking a major step towards improving the efficiency and capacity of Bangladesh’s principal maritime gateway.

CPA Chairman Rear Admiral SM Moniruzzaman signed the agreement on behalf of the Chittagong Port Authority, while DP World Chairman Essa Kazim signed on behalf of the international terminal operator at a ceremony held at Invest Bangladesh auditorium here.

Shipping Minister Sheikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for Shipping Md Rajib Ahsan, UAE Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdulla Ali Al Hamoudi and Invest Bangladesh Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, among others, attended the signing ceremony.

Under the concession, DP World will operate and manage NCT for an initial period of 15 years, while ownership of the terminal’s land, core infrastructure and assets will remain with CPA and, ultimately, the government of Bangladesh.

The agreement provides an upfront payment of around Tk 6 billion, with 25 per cent payable upon signing and the remaining 75 per cent before commencement of operations.

DP World will also invest more than Tk 10 billion during the first 10 years to modernise the terminal through new equipment, technology and operational improvements.

In addition, CPA will receive a share of terminal revenue or royalty, ranging from around 40 per cent to 67 per cent per TEU depending on average terminal revenue, along with a fixed annual fee of approximately Tk 100 million.

NCT handover to DP World sparks protest in capital, police baton-charge

The agreement includes a minimum annual volume guarantee of 1.23 million TEUs, with provision for adjustment to 1 million TEUs once a new terminal becomes operational.

Speaking at the ceremony, Shipping Minister Sheikh Rabiul Alam said the government’s objective was to rapidly increase the capacity and efficiency of existing strategic assets.

“Modern equipment, digital systems, international operating standards and global logistics connections will make NCT more competitive,” he said.

He said the government’s wider policy was to engage multiple international operators across terminals to improve service quality and reliability and strengthen supply-chain resilience.

DP World Chairman Essa Kazim said Bangladesh was becoming an increasingly important trading and manufacturing economy and DP World was committed to supporting its continued development.

“Through this partnership, DP World will connect the New Mooring Container Terminal to our global network of ports, logistics infrastructure and supply chain services, helping create more seamless links between Bangladesh and international markets,” he said.

He said the company would combine its operational expertise, technology and end-to-end logistics capabilities to support trade, attract investment and create new opportunities for businesses across Bangladesh.

CPA Chairman Rear Admiral Md Moniruzzaman said the partnership reflected Bangladesh’s commitment to strengthening its maritime and trade infrastructure through the public-private partnership framework.

He said the agreement would enhance operational performance, ease logistics constraints and strengthen connectivity with international markets.

item.title: Bangladesh signs 15-year deal with DP World to operate NCT
item.description:
Bangladesh on Thursday signed a 15-year agreement with UAE-based DP World to operate and maintain Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its overflow container yard.
The agreement was signed at 3:40pm.
Chittagong Port Authority Chairman Rear Admiral SM Moniruzzaman and DP World Chairman and CEO Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem signed the agreement.
The process of appointing an international operator for NCT began in 2019.
In March 2023, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs gave in-principle approval to appoint an international private operator under a public-private partnership framework.
The interim government later revived the initiative and selected DP World. However, the process stalled amid opposition and a workers’ strike earlier this year. The current government subsequently resumed negotiations.
Built in 2007 at a cost of around Tk2,000 crore, NCT has five jetties. Fourteen of Chittagong Port’s 18 quayside gantry cranes are located at the terminal.
More than 40% of the port’s container handling is carried out through NCT.
The project initially received in-principle approval from the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs in March 2023. The latest approval relates to the draft concession agreement governing the terminal’s operation and maintenance for 15 years.
Meanwhile, the Chittagong Port Protection Committee has been holding various programmes demanding the cancellation of the process to lease the terminal to a foreign company.

item.title: Salahuddin: Govt to set up two army camps in hills near Rohingya camps
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government has decided to set up two new army camps in the hilly areas adjacent to the Rohingya camps to prevent crimes including abductions.
He made the remarks to journalists at the Secretariat around 3pm on Thursday, after a meeting titled “Meeting for the Overall Improvement of Law and Order in Jungle Salimpur, Chittagong.”
The home minister said the two camps would be established in the hills of Rangikhali and Noakhalipara in Teknaf under the leadership of the 10th Infantry Division of Ramu.
He said abductions and other incidents occur regularly in the two hilly areas. To prevent these crimes, a decision has been made to set up two camps in the area under the leadership of the 10th Infantry Division.
The meeting expressed the view that once the two camps are established, such crimes in the area will be eliminated.
He said joint operations are conducted to address the law and order situation inside and outside the Rohingya camps. These operations are being carried out against various crimes, including drugs, weapons and human trafficking.
A deputy inspector general (DIG) of the Armed Police Battalion leads the operations, with other law enforcement agencies also involved.
The home minister also mentioned a decision to rebuild the fencing, or barbed-wire barrier, to strengthen security at the Rohingya camps.
In addition, solar-powered lighting will be arranged outside the camps. Closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras will be installed at fixed intervals, and control towers and watchtowers will be built.
He further said that in the event of a war or any emergency, the army will lead the response. A Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) has been set for this purpose.

item.title: Russian strike on buses kills 30 in frontline Ukrainian city
item.description:
Ukraine on Thursday accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after 30 people were killed when two buses were blown up in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, in one of the deadliest single attacks for weeks.
Photos posted by local authorities showed the burnt-out metal shell of the vehicles, with the blurred-out images of bodies and debris strewn across the road.
Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb.
The strikes come just a day after five children were among 22 killed when a Russian missile struck a five-story apartment block in Pryluky, in the northern Chernigiv region.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” Donetsk Governor Vadym Filashkin said, accusing Moscow of flouting “every conceivable rule of warfare and norm of international humanitarian law.”
Kramatorsk City Council called it “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population.”
“Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added.
There has been mounting concern about the increase in civilian casualties in the conflict, as both sides step up long-range attacks beyond their borders.
Since Russia first invaded in 2022, Ukraine has accused its forces of deliberately attacking and killing civilians.
The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths throughout the war, but says the real number is considerably higher.
Last week, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had sanctioned massive attacks on civilian areas.
The Kremlin has denied the claim.
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, has come under increasing attack, including on Wednesday when Russia launched a barrage of powerful ballistic and cruise missiles, and fast-moving, jet-powered drones.
The city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said two people were found dead on Thursday after a fire at a four-story building that was hit by a drone in the densely populated Solomyansky district.
Klitschko has said the attacks, which have hit key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid, were “tearing Kyiv apart.”
For the first few years of the war, Kyiv had been relatively spared from the devastation wrought on the frontline but should now be on a war footing, he argued.
Kramatorsk, which was home to some 150,000 people before the war, is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as its own.
It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” which troops are fighting to keep hold of.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern fringes, which has prompted calls for the civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
Filashkin said Thursday’s strike, which happened at 10am (0700 GMT), represented a “sharp deterioration” in security and ordered the suspension of public transport in Kramatorsk and neighboring Sloviansk.
“Under these circumstances, we cannot risk the lives of passengers and drivers,” he said. “The safety of the residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is now our top priority.”
Ukraine last month launched a counter-offensive against Russian troops around Lyman -- to the north of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk -- claiming some success in regaining pockets of territory.

item.description:
An attack on Riyadh’s international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded 309 others, some of them seriously, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation officials said on Saturday, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to vow on Sunday a decisive response against Yemen’s Houthis.

Four Saudi citizens were among the dead, as well as two Bangladeshis, one US citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the statement added.

The coalition blamed the group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.

Earlier in the day, authorities had suspended operations at Riyadh’s international airport. The Saudi civil aviation authority had initially confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the “serious emergency”, a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility.

Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday.

Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said 155 arriving and 161 departing flights had been cancelled, while a total of 222 flights were delayed.

At around 6pm local time, Flightradar24 noted that flights bound for the airport were “diverting elsewhere, mainly to Jeddah at the moment”. It later shared a notice to airmen (Notam) for operations suspended till 12am.

A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic.

“I was on gate 403” at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP. “I saw 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”

A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday.

“We were told we are dealing with a ‘serious emergency situation’. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh”, with many in critical condition, the source said.

The aviation authority said the number of injured from the attack was still being assessed, adding that airport “operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities”.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July.

A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with “dozens of people injured” in all.

A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass. Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.

Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Makkah had been injured while waiting to board their flight.

A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by “a missile around 3:00pm” (5pm PKT).

“Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target,” the source said.

‘War crime’

Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki described the strike as a “cowardly terrorist attack” against a civilian facility.

“The cowardly terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia… which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” he said in a statement on X.

US ‘may’ join Saudi strikes

Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, US President Donald Trump said: “We may.”

He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in Saudi Arabia “not acceptable”.

US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for US military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.

Embassy warnings

The Yemen conflict flared back to life after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle Eastern war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.

The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war in the region.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen’s government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour’s civil war.

Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.

The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware of attacks” on Riyadh airport on Saturday and called on American citizens to avoid the area.

The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Spain’s embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a “new attack… by the Houthis”.

A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies “indicated that they had decided to prohibit their staff’s travel to/from Riyadh Airport over the next week as a prudential step”.

Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station.

Yemen fighting

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-led government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.

The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country’s entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.

The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area — a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping — but they claimed to have repelled the assault.

Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

item.title: New Ganges waters treaty with guarantee clause emerges as priority for Dhaka
item.description:
Securing its fair share of the transboundary rivers' waters is likely to become a major issue for Bangladesh in the coming days, making effective water diplomacy, international cooperation and constructive engagement with India increasingly important, officials and experts have said.
The urgency is underscored by the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, signed on December 12, 1996, which is due to expire on the same date this year. The government in Dhaka has been increasingly vocal in recent weeks, communicating a vision that Bangladesh will be seeking a new or revised agreement that safeguards its interests, particularly its share of dry-season flows, with the inclusion of a guarantee clause.
“Water could emerge as one of the major challenges for the entire world, including Bangladesh, in the future,” said Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan on Thursday, stressing the need to integrate proper water management into national development planning.
Bangladesh and India share 54 transboundary rivers, but the Ganges remains the only one covered by a bilateral water-sharing agreement between the two countries.
Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee said Bangladesh wants a new or revised Ganges agreement rather than simply renewing the existing treaty, with provisions guaranteeing its required share of water during the dry season.
“Our main priority will be to bring back the guarantee clause that was included in the 1977 agreement,” he said on Thursday.
The 1977 agreement, negotiated by the BNP's founder Ziaur Rahman, included a safeguard stipulating that if the Ganges flow at Farakka fell below the level projected in the treaty to be provided to Bangladesh as its scheduled share during any 10-day period, the release to Bangladesh would not fall below 80% of that share.
An official also referred to Article III of the 1977 agreement, which stipulated that water released to Bangladesh at Farakka should not be reduced below Farakka, except for India's reasonable water uses, not exceeding 200 cusecs, between Farakka and the point where both banks of the Ganges lie within Bangladesh.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh would seek an outcome that safeguards its national interests and security, including through a possible guarantee clause.
Asked whether the existing treaty would be renewed or replaced with a new agreement, he said, “Whatever is best for Bangladesh’s interest will be done.”
Kobir said Bangladesh’s committee was ready and Dhaka was awaiting a final response from its Indian counterparts.
“Our committee is ready. We are just waiting for the final response from our Indian counterparts. So yes, we are hopeful,” he said.
He also stressed that international law was being taken into consideration in addressing the water-sharing issues.
The Indian government, through its Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal has said that issues concerning the Ganges treaty and other shared rivers would be discussed through the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC).
“On the Ganga Water Treaty, as also other rivers that we share between Bangladesh and India, we have a Joint Rivers Commission. All matters relating to rivers, river-related matters, will be discussed as part of this Joint Rivers Commission,” he said recently, adding that technical-level meetings on the Ganges treaty had continued.
Kobir said sincerity at the political and official levels in both countries was essential to finding an amicable resolution to the long-standing water-sharing issues.
He expressed optimism that the issues could be resolved positively if the leadership of both countries demonstrated a willingness to cooperate.
Anee said water diplomacy should focus on cooperation and mutual benefits rather than competition, stressing the need for sustained dialogue, scientific cooperation, data sharing and inclusive water governance.
“Cooperation should create mutual benefits rather than being framed explicitly as a competition over water,” he said.
He described water as closely linked to Bangladesh’s geography, economy, agriculture, culture, foreign policy and national security.
“We are a delta country shaped by rivers. Yet, we are also a riparian country dependent on water flows originating beyond our borders,” he said.
Anee called for stronger engagement through the JRC and multilateral water governance mechanisms, alongside greater international cooperation and scientific collaboration.
Bangladesh has joined the UN Water Convention, while the Delta Plan 2100 and national river-management initiatives provide a broader framework for addressing long-term water challenges.
“We need cooperation instead of confrontation, evidence instead of assumptions, participation instead of execution, and long-term planning instead of short-term responses,” he said.
“Our goal should not simply be to manage water crises when they occur; our goal should be to build a just, decent, and cooperative water future,” Anee added, calling for greater youth participation in water governance.
Turning to the Teesta, Anee said the river was particularly important for people in northern Bangladesh, where seasonal variations cause water shortages during the dry season and erosion and flooding during the monsoon.
He said the government had placed considerable emphasis on the Teesta project, with feasibility studies and technical assistance underway.
State Minister Kobir also highlighted the importance of water diplomacy on multilateral platforms, stronger international partnerships, technology transfer and scientific cooperation to advance Bangladesh’s interests in transboundary water management.
With the Ganges treaty approaching expiry, Bangladesh faces the task of securing an equitable and sustainable water-sharing arrangement while strengthening cooperation on other shared rivers.
“I think it is very important for Bangladesh and India to renew the Ganges Treaty. But it has to be revised. The very simple reason is that the treaty was done almost three decades ago,” international affairs expert Prof Shahab Enam Khan told UNB recently.
Shahab, who is the executive director of Bangladesh Center for Indo-Pacific Affairs, strongly suggested that this should also come with arrangements such as revitalising the JRC and including a much more transparent and accountable data-sharing system, which will definitely build much more confidence over "hydro-diplomacy" and water management and water sharing, most importantly, between the two countries.
“This is very important that we should also go into the diplomatic negotiations not only from the diplomatic perspective, but also from engineering, science, and definitely economic perspectives,” he said.
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur, while attending the ninth Indian Ocean Conference in Mauritius, said they would like to see that there is an arrangement and a new treaty, or a revised treaty, ensuring the essential needs of their people.
“These are common rivers, and we have common legacies here, common interests and, as I said, there's no other alternative but to seek a solution that is durable and will win public trust. And this will also be very important to lay the basis for the relationship over the next 25 to 50 years,” he told NDTV on the sidelines of the conference.
The foreign minister said they have done 55 years (of bilateral relations) already. “So, I don't think we should look at five years or ten years. We have to look at the very long term. So, mutual climate resilience as a priority in our foreign policies, our people policy, I should say, will actually be a key driver of the future.”

item.title: US announces sanctions on the International Criminal Court
item.description:
US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize.
This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a “sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court.”
The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court’s arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Since 2020 and the back end of Trump’s first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that “deprioritize” alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them.
“President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said in a statement.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” he said.
Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said “only President Trump” resolved to take action.
“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court,” Rubio said. “If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”
The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN’s members.
“The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions.
The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a “collective promise” that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished.
“That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it,” the court said. It appealed to members to take “concrete actions” to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work.
“No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice,” it said. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack.”
A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their “continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC.”
“As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States,” the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said.
They said that, despite the ICC’s best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions “will have a significant impact on the Court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its “leadership” in issuing the sanctions.
“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” he said.
The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012.
Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift.
Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year’s laureate.
“The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” the Committee wrote.
It said judges like Pillay “guard the thin red line between order and chaos,” but lamented that “today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked.” The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague.
It’s the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression.
The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute.
More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it.
Several of the world’s most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court’s jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute.
A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it.
That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians.
The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump’s second term.
Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, “America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution.”
He argued it was possible for US “soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders” to be “dragged before an international court” and tried by judges “from random countries across the globe.”
Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela’s new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC.
A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request.
The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC’s chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court.
In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC’s president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court.

Four people died of dengue, and 1,631 were hospitalized with the Aedes mosquito-borne disease in the last 24 hours till 8am on Saturday, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
With this development, the country has recorded 299 deaths from dengue this year.
Of the new dengue cases, 703 were recorded in Dhaka division, 61 in Mymensingh division, 234 in Chittagong division, 184 in Khulna division, 141 in Rajshahi division, 75 in Rangpur division, 219 in Barisal division and 14 in Sylhet division.
A total of 97,082 dengue patients have so far been hospitalized across the country this year, according to the DGHS report.
However, in the last 24 hours, 1,627 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals.
So far, 91,007 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment this year.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

item.title: Bangladesh discusses €250 million loan for women's health initiative
item.description:
Bangladesh discussed a proposed €250 million loan from the European Investment Bank (EIB) to implement a women's health initiative with international development partners during the World Health Summit (WHS) 2026 in Berlin, Germany, on Saturday.
The bilateral and technical discussions took place at the Charité campus in Berlin, involving a high-level delegation from the Bangladesh government and international development partners.
The Bangladesh delegation was led by Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Health Ziauddin Hyder.
The proposed Women's Health Initiative aims to reduce maternal mortality, ensure early detection of cervical and breast cancers, and develop modern facilities to provide round-the-clock emergency obstetric services at the union level.
The discussions also covered strengthening district hospitals and introducing a digital patient-tracking system.
The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, and the Berlin Institute of Health (BIH) are providing technical and strategic support for the initiative.
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said: “This international partnership will play an important role in ensuring quality healthcare for women and girls in remote areas of Bangladesh.”
The Bangladesh delegation also visited Charité Hospital in Berlin to observe its medical facilities and cancer screening services.
The parties agreed to form a joint working group to support the future development of healthcare systems in both countries.

item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-AIRPORT

The third attack this week on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left at least 12 people dead and more than 300 wounded, Saudi authorities said, as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.

The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, officials said, 309 were wounded.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.

Saudi Arabia says 3 dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks

Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. This week's two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

The deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

A Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond to the attack.

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.

All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport". The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.

US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life."

Eyewitness saw wounded on the ground

One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

The US embassy in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.

The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

Riyadh due to hold major summits

Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organizers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.

item.title: Rooppur nuclear power plant begins fission, moves closer to electricity generation
item.description:
The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has begun a nuclear fission reaction, bringing Bangladesh’s only nuclear power plant closer to starting electricity generation and supplying power to the national grid.

The reaction is the process through which nuclear energy is released and marks a crucial stage in the final preparations for electricity generation and supply. The plant is scheduled to supply 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid in December.

According to sources at the Rooppur plant, the process of generating energy through nuclear fission was initially scheduled to begin in September. However, the schedule was delayed after defects were detected during tests of safety valves. The valves were tested under high pressure in two rounds last week. After reviewing the test results, the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) approved the start of the reaction last Thursday. Nuclear fission began at 3:34pm on Sunday.

The Rooppur project in Pabna is the largest single project in Bangladesh’s history in terms of cost. The Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, is implementing the project. The state-owned Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL), under the commission, is responsible for operating the plant.

Russian contractor Atomstroyexport is constructing two units at Rooppur, each with a capacity of 1,200 megawatts.

NPCBL Managing Director Md Zahedul Hasan told Prothom Alo that the final process leading to the start of the nuclear reaction began on Saturday after three days of preparation. The controlled reaction successfully started on Sunday.

“This brings to an end the long wait following the beginning of Bangladesh’s journey towards the peaceful use of nuclear energy in 1961. This is a major milestone for the country’s science sector,” he said.

Sources at the plant said the reactor vessel of the first unit had achieved criticality for the first time. This is a significant milestone for Bangladesh’s nuclear power programme. Following criticality, all key reactor parameters have remained within the prescribed limits, and the process is being conducted under controlled conditions.

Officials involved in the project said the start of the nuclear reaction was a major step towards connecting the plant to the national grid. The next stages will involve reactor physics tests, verification of safety systems, a gradual increase in reactor power and the completion of tests and preparations required for grid connection, in accordance with the approved commissioning programme.

Each stage must comply with the highest safety standards, approved procedures and regulatory requirements.

According to plant officials, achieving reactor criticality is not merely a technical success but also a historic recognition of Bangladesh’s capabilities in science, engineering and nuclear technology. After years of effort, the country has reached a crucial stage in connecting its first nuclear power plant to the national grid.

Reaction process likely to take 30 to 40 days

Sources at the Rooppur plant said a series of tests would be conducted following the start of the nuclear reaction. The entire process could take 30 to 40 days.

The reactor’s power output will then be increased gradually. Nuclear fuel fission will generate heat, which will be used to produce steam and drive a turbine to generate electricity.

Once the reactor begins producing energy, electricity can be supplied to the national grid when its output reaches 30 per cent of capacity. At that stage, the plant is expected to supply 300 megawatts of electricity, potentially in December.

Plant officials said trial operations could continue for seven to eight months after the initial start-up. Once electricity is supplied to the grid, Bangladesh will become the world’s 33rd country to generate nuclear power.

Rooppur was recognised as a nuclear installation after nuclear fuel arrived at the project site in October 2023. With the receipt of the fuel, Bangladesh also joined the group of countries possessing nuclear energy capabilities.
According to plant sources, once operational, the nuclear power plant will be able to supply electricity continuously at a steady rate, 24 hours a day.

The reactor will require refuelling every 18 months. A unit may remain shut down for up to two months for the removal of spent fuel, loading of fresh fuel and maintenance.

The sources said that once one unit of Rooppur became operational, it could save USD 1 billion annually in fuel imports. However, the project has already been delayed by three and a half years.

Project cost rises by Tk 260 billion


The Rooppur project was originally scheduled to run until December 2025. Its deadline has been extended twice, with the latest completion date set for June 2028.

Although the deadline has been extended under the agreement with the contractor, there is no provision to increase the project cost under that agreement. However, the rise in the dollar exchange rate has increased the project's expenses by Tk 260 billion.

The total cost of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is now expected to reach Tk 1.39 trillion.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,162 as seven die in 24 hours
item.description:
Seven more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Sunday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,162.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all seven of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,058, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the seven new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in the Sylhet division with three deaths, while Sunamganj district recorded the highest district-level death count with two casualties.
A total of 1,180 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Sunday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 205,028.
During the same period, 93 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 22,421.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 182,047 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 174,469 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Bangladesh plans €250m investment in women's health
item.description:
Bangladesh’s planned €250 million investment in women’s health aimed to target approximately 47 million women and girls over five years, highlighted at the opening press conference of the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin on Sunday where global health leaders gathered to discuss ways to build more resilient and equitable healthcare systems.
The Government of Bangladesh and the European Investment Bank (EIB) have set out plans to redirect the financing under an existing EIB sovereign loan towards the Women’s Health Initiative, which is expected to run from 2027 to 2031.
The program aims to expand access to maternal and newborn healthcare, cervical and breast cancer services, and emergency obstetric and newborn care.
It will also support stronger primary healthcare, referral services, district hospitals and critical care facilities.
Sardar Md Sakhawat Hussain, Bangladesh’s health and family welfare minister, said the initiative reflected the government’s commitment to building a stronger and more equitable health system according to a latest release by UNFPA.
“The health and well-being of women and girls are fundamental to Bangladesh’s future,” he said.
“This initiative reflects our determination to build a stronger and more equitable health system, one that prioritizes prevention and protects women throughout their lives.”
He added that the partnership with the EIB and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) would help ensure quality healthcare services reached communities across the country.
Dr Ziauddin Hyder, special adviser to the prime minister on health, said the investment would support a broader shift in the country’s healthcare approach.
“Our vision is to shift health systems from treatment to prevention and health promotion, and this new investment will help drive that national vision forward,” he said.
The €250 million program is designed to address gaps in women’s healthcare while improving the capacity of the wider health system.
Its key priorities include expanding maternal and newborn care, strengthening cervical and breast cancer services, improving access to emergency obstetric and newborn care, and upgrading primary healthcare, referral services, district hospitals and critical care facilities.
The initiative is expected to benefit approximately 47 million women and girls between 2027 and 2031.
UNFPA Executive Director Diene Keita said women’s health remained critically underfunded despite its importance to sustainable development.
“This landmark investment shows how national leadership and innovative development financing can combine proven strategies to accelerate progress at scale,” she said at the opening press conference of WHS 2026 on Sunday.
Keita added that UNFPA would contribute its expertise and longstanding presence in Bangladesh to help ensure the program delivered measurable and equitable improvements in the health of millions of women and girls.
“We need to shift the way we view women’s health: from cost to investment, from a niche sector to a national economic priority,” Keita said highlighting Bangladesh’s initiative.
She described investment in women’s health as an investment in a country’s people, productivity and future, adding that Bangladesh’s initiative could serve as an example for other countries.
The World Health Summit 2026, running from October 11 to 13 under the theme “From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health,” brings together more than 4,000 participants on-site and tens of thousands online, with over 400 speakers across more than 75 sessions.
